summary: Fort Point Light, at the mouth of the Penobscot River: an 1836 granite light, the brick tower of 1857, a fog bell, automated in 1988, now in a state park.

access.note: Fort Point State Park is open daily 9 a.m. to sunset. The tower is closed.

facts.agency: Maine Bureau of Parks and Lands (Fort Point State Park)

events.note: Conical granite tower and dwelling; USLHS gives 1837 as the establishment year

Inspector found the dwelling walls cracked on all four sides and the tower cracked from roof to base (per LighthouseFriends). The year is inferred: LighthouseFriends says 'a mere six years later' than the 1836 house, so 1842 is not a dated source statement.
Light-House Board judged the station entirely worn out and asked Congress for $5,000 to rebuild it
New square brick tower and keeper's house replaced the granite tower
Fourth-order Fresnel lens in the new tower
Bell house built in 1890; the Board's report for 1891 records a 1,200-pound bell provided for the station
Oil house built (Light-House Board, scan 294; nomination)
The Fort Point Hotel on the point burned the night of 7 June 1898; the keeper's report and the Ellsworth American both record it
Dwelling interior rearranged; three dormer windows built
Fog bell disabled 15 March and back in working order 17 March 1899
Light electrified, brought up to 4,500 candlepower
Coast Guard automated the light in October 1988; last keeper Larry Baum
Coast Guard leased the station to the Maine Bureau of Parks and Lands
Deed transferred to the State of Maine under the Maine Lights Program

corrections.proposed: tower, brick, square, built 1857, 9.5 m (31 ft), standing; the 1836 granite conical tower was replaced
corrections.why: The brick tower standing today was built in 1857 (NRHP; LighthouseFriends; USLHS 'Year Tower Established: 1857'). The 1836 tower was conical granite (LighthouseFriends).
The Light-House Board's reports record a fog bell at the station: a 1,200-pound bell provided in the 1891 report and a fog bell disabled and restored in March 1899.
USLHS gives 1988 as the year automated; LighthouseFriends says the Coast Guard automated the station in October 1988; Maine Lights Today also gives 1988.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: USLHS gives 1837 as the establishment year. NRHP and LighthouseFriends give 1836 for the first light, so the story uses 1836 for the first tower.
NRHP gives 26 ft from base to lantern centre for the 1857 tower. LighthouseFriends and Maine Lights Today give 31 ft. The story uses 31 ft and notes the difference.

notes_for_editor: Keepers come from the USLHS roster (NARA registers via the Kraig Anderson inventory), matched to the station by name and position (0.06 km); not yet confirmed in primary records. Contractor George W. Pendexter is not a keeper and is not listed. The archive gives Wayne McGraw an end year only, Harry H. Lahaye a start in the 1970s with no end, and Eugene R. Benner at least 1970. Tower height: NRHP gives 26 ft from base to lantern centre for the 1857 tower; LighthouseFriends and Maine Lights Today give 31 ft (the record's 9.5 m). The story gives 31 ft and notes NRHP's 26 ft. Establishment year: USLHS 1837; NRHP and LighthouseFriends 1836. The Board's 1891 entry (scan 51) is OCR'd with a garbled entry number and bell line; the quoted words are the readable part. The 1897 oil-house line (scan 294) is OCR'd as 'oil Louse'; the NRHP date (1897) supports it. LighthouseFriends names the hotel 'Wassaumkeag' and dates it to 1872; the Stockton Springs town history dates an elegant hotel of that name to 1895. The sources were not reconciled; the story does not depend on which is right. LighthouseFriends spells the 1850 keeper Bowdin in one passage and Bowden elsewhere; the roster has Bowden. Life-Saving Service entries for 'Fort Point' in the corpus are Fort Point, California, not this station. James H. Perry appears at Curtis Island (1962-1964) and here (1964-1966) under one archive person slug; the join is the archive's, and no other_stations entry is made. The NRHP listing date (1988-03-23 in the record) was not checked against the nomination form. The record's focal height (26.8 m) is from USLHS (88 ft) but was not in the text read, so it is not in facts. The record's characteristic (F W) and range (15 nm) are not in any source read here. Verification 2026-10-22: scan pages checked with corpus.py page and the cached OCR. FY1891 entry 'Fort Painty, mouth of Penobscot River' is at printed p.40 (scan p.51); its item number and the bell line are garbled, and the readable words (1,200-pound bell struck by machinery; minor repairs to dwelling and tower) match. FY1893 p.55, FY1897 p.294 ('oil Louse'), FY1899 pp.35 and 79 match. The Ellsworth American page (sp=8) reads 'The large summer hotel at Fort Point... was burned last night... The hotel will not be rebuilt.'; its loss estimate is OCR'd as '*45,000' and was left out. The town's 1895 hotel date and LighthouseFriends' 1872 date are stated as a disagreement in the story. Page images were not viewed. The FY1891 Board entry (scan p.51) is read from cached OCR, where the item number is garbled and the bell figure appears as 'l,200-pound'; the 1,200-pound reading and the 'minor repairs' line are consistent with the Board's other entries on the same pages, but an editor should check the image before relying on the figure. The archive's Harry H. Lahaye span ('1970s-') is recorded as from 1970, approximate.
